\begin{abstract}
Multimodal retrieval-augmented generation can answer a document question from optical character
recognition (OCR) text, a retrieved page image, or both, at different GPU cost, which makes serving it at scale a
GPU provisioning problem. We measure this trade-off end to end and test whether a router can exploit it. On one
RTX 4090, every path is run on 8,150 DocVQA and InfographicVQA questions with BM25 and ColPali retrieval and
one shared generator, measuring average normalised Levenshtein similarity (ANLS), GPU-seconds, energy and latency.
The page image alone is the strongest fixed policy; adding the OCR text costs 1.6$\times$ its GPU time for
little gain. The Cost-Aware Visual Router (CAVR) chooses the path per query under a cost weight set per deployment.
Its content-aware variant CAVR-CE, a cross-encoder (CE) over the retrieved passages, uses 29\% less GPU
compute than always combining both contexts at 0.008 lower ANLS, and keeps a 35\% saving on
1,499 questions from the datasets' training splits. Against the page image alone, routing is not consistently
better: CAVR-CE gains 0.016 ANLS for 15\% more GPU compute on the design splits, but only 0.005
(not significant) on the training-split questions, which ColPali and possibly the generator saw in training. Served
live with vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs, CAVR-CE sustained 1.82$\times$ the arrival rate of
always-hybrid at a p95 latency of 5\,s; a simulator driven by measured service times overestimated absolute capacity
by 1.4--2.0$\times$, so its GPU counts for larger pools are projections. Our earlier
keyword-rule labels agree with measured outcomes no better than chance.
\end{abstract}
